channel.title: Chiba on Japan Specialty Traveler
channel.description: Recent content in Chiba on Japan Specialty Traveler

item.title: Boso Flower Fields Guide: Minamiboso Blooms & Access
item.description: Thanks to its mild, frost-free maritime climate, the southern tip of the Boso Peninsula bursts into flower while much of Japan is still cold — making Minamiboso and Tateyama a beloved late-winter and spring flower destination. Along the scenic Boso Flower Line coastal road, fields glow with poppies, rapeseed, stocks and marigolds, and “flower-picking gardens” let visitors pick their own blooms to take home from as early as January. Set between blue Pacific coastline and the green slopes near Mount Nokogiri, the flower fields make a colourful, family-friendly day out and one of the prettiest spring drives near Tokyo.

item.title: Boso Peninsula Cycling Guide: Coastal Routes & Access
item.description: With its mild climate, gentle terrain and long stretches of quiet coast, the Boso Peninsula is one of the best places near Tokyo for cycling. Riders can roll for kilometres beside the Pacific along the Kujukuri coast, climb to flower fields and capes in the south, or pedal sleepy inland lanes past rice paddies and old towns. The famously flat Kujukuri cycling path is ideal for beginners, while the southern Boso’s coastal roads reward stronger riders with sea views and the Boso Flower Line.

item.title: Boso Sea Kayaking Guide: Tours, Caves & Access
item.description: The clear, sheltered waters and rugged little coves of the southern Boso Peninsula make it one of the best places near Tokyo to try sea kayaking. Guided tours paddle out from spots around Tateyama and Minamiboso to explore turquoise coves, slip into sea caves, glide past rocky islets and, on calm days, peer down at fish and coral over the gunwale. Beginner-friendly tours with stable double kayaks and instruction make it accessible to first-timers and families, while the warm Kuroshio current keeps the water inviting from spring through autumn.

item.title: Chiba Castle Guide: Museum, Cherry Blossoms & Access
item.description: In the heart of Chiba City, Chiba Castle crowns the leafy Inohana hill where the powerful Chiba clan once ruled the region in the medieval era. The handsome white keep you see today is a modern reconstruction housing the Chiba City Folk Museum, which traces the clan’s history and local samurai culture. Surrounded by Inohana Park — one of the city’s best cherry-blossom spots — and close to the venerable Chiba Shrine, it makes an easy, pleasant half-day of history, greenery and city sightseeing right by central Chiba.

item.title: Chiba Peanuts Guide: Japan's Top Peanuts, Sweets & Where to Buy
item.description: Chiba is Japan’s peanut capital, producing the lion’s share of the country’s domestic crop — and “Chiba peanuts” are a prized, premium souvenir nationwide. The sandy soils around Yachimata and the Boso interior yield famously sweet, fragrant nuts that locals enjoy in every form: freshly boiled (yude-rakkasei) in autumn, classic roasted, ground into nutty peanut confections, and even as peanut soft-serve ice cream. From specialty shops and roadside stands to elegant gift boxes, peanuts here are a genuine regional craft.

item.title: Choshi Guide: Cape Inubo, Soy Sauce & Seafood Access
item.description: At the far northeastern tip of Chiba, the port city of Choshi is where the Tone River meets the Pacific — a place famous for three things: soy sauce, seafood and sunrises. Pounded by the open ocean, Cape Inubosaki is one of the first places in mainland Japan to see the New Year’s sunrise, marked by a handsome white lighthouse you can climb. Choshi is also one of Japan’s great soy sauce towns (home to Yamasa and Higeta), where you can tour breweries and taste the difference, and one of its busiest fishing ports, serving superb sashimi and grilled fish.

item.title: Choshi Whale & Dolphin Watching Guide: Tours & Access
item.description: Few people realise you can go whale and dolphin watching within easy reach of Tokyo — but the rich waters off Choshi, where the warm Kuroshio current meets the cold Oyashio off the Boso Peninsula’s northeastern tip, are one of Japan’s most reliable spots. Boat tours head out from Choshi port to look for large pods of dolphins (often hundreds at a time) and, in season, whales such as minke, Bryde’s and even sperm whales.

item.title: Isumi Railway Guide: Rapeseed Flowers, Trains & Access
item.description: The Isumi Railway is one of Chiba’s most photogenic country railways — a single-carriage local line winding through the rural heart of the Boso Peninsula. It’s most famous in spring, when the tracks are framed by ribbons of golden rapeseed blossom (nanohana) and pink cherry trees, drawing photographers to capture the little train rolling through a sea of yellow. Cute themed services (including Moomin-decorated trains and a dining “restaurant train”) add to the charm.

item.title: Izumi Nature Park Cherry Blossom Guide: Sakura & Access
item.description: When spring arrives in the rural Boso interior, Izumi Nature Park near Sosa becomes one of Chiba’s loveliest cherry-blossom (sakura) spots — a quiet expanse of ponds, woods and meadows where rows of cherry trees bloom alongside golden rapeseed flowers for a classic pink-and-yellow spring scene. Far from the city crowds, it’s a peaceful place for hanami picnics, gentle walks and birdwatching, and it pairs perfectly with the Isumi Railway, whose little trains roll through the same flower-filled countryside.

item.title: Kashiwa Reysol Guide: J-League Match & Access
item.description: For football fans visiting the Tokyo area, a Kashiwa Reysol match offers one of the most authentic and atmospheric ways to experience Japanese J-League soccer. The club plays at the compact Hitachi Kashiwa Stadium (Sankyo Frontier Kashiwa Stadium) — a rare football-specific ground in Japan where steep, close stands put you right on top of the action, and the passionate “yellow” supporters keep up nonstop drumming, chanting and flag-waving for 90 minutes.

item.title: Katsuura Big Hina Matsuri Guide: Doll Festival & Access
item.description: Every late winter, the seaside town of Katsuura stages one of Japan’s most photogenic doll festivals — the Katsuura Big Hina Matsuri. For Hinamatsuri (the Girls' Day / Doll Festival), the town displays tens of thousands of hina dolls all over town, most spectacularly cascading down the 60 stone steps of Tomisaki Shrine in a tiered pyramid of pink and gold. Lit up in the evenings and set against the fishing-town backdrop, the spectacle draws photographers and families from across the country, making it a magical early-spring day trip on the Boso coast.

item.title: Katsuura Katsuo (Bonito) Guide: What to Eat & Access
item.description: The Boso port of Katsuura lands some of Japan’s finest katsuo (skipjack bonito) — a fish so central to the town that it even shares its name (katsuo-ura). Riding the warm Kuroshio current, fat spring “first bonito” (hatsu-gatsuo) and rich autumn “returning bonito” (modori-gatsuo) come ashore here at their peak. The classic way to enjoy it is katsuo no tataki — fillets seared over straw so the outside is smoky and the inside stays ruby-rare — served with ginger, garlic, and ponzu.

item.title: Katsuura Morning Market & Sashimi Guide: What to Eat & Access
item.description: The fishing town of Katsuura on the Boso coast is a paradise for seafood lovers, home to one of Japan’s three great morning markets — a tradition running for over 400 years. Each morning, stalls along the old streets brim with the night’s catch, vegetables and pickles, and nearby diners serve glistening sashimi rice bowls and set meals built around the day’s freshest fish straight off the boats. Katsuura is also the surprising birthplace of fiery Katsuura tantanmen, a local spicy ramen.

item.title: Kisarazu Fireworks Guide: Summer Hanabi & Access
item.description: Each summer, the bayside city of Kisarazu lights up the night with one of inner Tokyo Bay’s biggest fireworks festivals (hanabi) — a beloved August tradition that sends tens of thousands of shells bursting over the water. Held along the Kisarazu waterfront near the foot of the Aqua-Line, the display reflects spectacularly off the bay and draws huge crowds in summer yukata to picnic, snack at festival stalls and watch the sky erupt in colour.

item.title: Kujukuri Beach Guide: Japan's Longest Beach & Access
item.description: Stretching some 60 kilometres in a near-straight line down Chiba’s Pacific coast, Kujukuri Beach is one of the longest beaches in Japan — an immense ribbon of sand, surf and big sky. Its name (“99 ri”) nods to its legendary length, and its open eastern aspect makes it a famous spot to watch the sunrise over the ocean. Long a centre of the iwashi (sardine) fishing industry, today it’s a summer playground for swimming, surfing, beachcombing and seaside seafood, with a refreshingly wild, uncommercialised feel.

item.title: Kujukuri Surfing Guide: Beaches, Lessons & Access
item.description: Chiba’s Pacific-facing Kujukuri coast is one of the Tokyo area’s great surfing zones — a 60-kilometre run of open sand that catches consistent ocean swell from multiple directions. Towns like Ichinomiya (host to Olympic surfing in 2021), Katakai and Taito are packed with surf shops, schools and a laid-back board culture, making it an excellent place to learn or to chase clean waves close to the capital. With sandy beach breaks suited to beginners, lessons and rentals readily available, and reliable surf from spring through autumn, Kujukuri is where many Tokyoites learn to ride — and a fun, sporty addition to a Chiba coast trip.

item.title: Makuhari Messe Guide: Events, Expos & Access
item.description: Makuhari Messe, in the Bayfront business district of Chiba, is one of Japan’s largest convention and exhibition centres — and a magnet for international fans of Japanese pop culture. Designed by architect Fumihiko Maki and opened in 1989, its vast halls and event arena host an extraordinary calendar: blockbuster anime, manga and gaming expos, music concerts and festivals, motor and tech trade shows, and major sporting events. For overseas visitors, it’s the venue behind many bucket-list events, and its location between Tokyo and Narita Airport — with a cluster of hotels, malls and a beach park nearby — makes it remarkably convenient to attend.

item.title: Mount Nokogiri Guide: Hell Lookout, Great Buddha & Access
item.description: Rising straight from the sea on the Boso Peninsula, Mount Nokogiri (Nokogiri-yama, “Saw Mountain”) is one of Chiba’s most spectacular day trips — a former quarry whose jagged, sawtooth cliffs now host the sprawling temple grounds of Nihon-ji. Here you’ll find the thrilling Jigoku-nozoki (“Hell Lookout”), an overhanging rock platform with a dizzying drop and sweeping views over Tokyo Bay to Mt. Fuji, plus Japan’s largest pre-modern stone Buddha, the serene 31-metre Nihon-ji Daibutsu, and the moss-covered ranks of the Thousand Buddhas.

item.title: Narita Unagi Guide: Best Eel Restaurants & Access
item.description: The temple town of Narita is one of the best places near Tokyo to feast on unagi (freshwater eel) — a tradition stretching back centuries to feed pilgrims visiting Narita-san. Along the atmospheric Omotesando approach to the temple, dozens of long-established eel restaurants fillet, skewer and grill eel fresh to order, often in full view of the street, then glaze it in sweet-savoury tare sauce over rice as unadon or unaju.

item.title: Narita-san Shinshoji Temple Guide: Access from the Airport & Tips
item.description: Just minutes from Narita Airport, Narita-san Shinshoji Temple is one of the most important and atmospheric Buddhist temples in the Tokyo area — the perfect first or last stop on a trip to Japan. Founded in 940 and headquarters of the Shingon Chisan sect, it enshrines Fudo Myo-o, the fierce, flame-wreathed guardian deity, and draws millions of worshippers a year (it ranks among Japan’s busiest for New Year’s visits). Spread across a hillside of grand halls, a soaring pagoda and a tranquil landscaped park, and approached by a charming old street of eel restaurants and souvenir shops, it offers a deep dose of living Japanese tradition right by the airport.

item.title: Naritasan Calligraphy Guide: Shodo Experience & Access
item.description: The temple town of Narita is a wonderful place to try shodo (Japanese calligraphy) — the meditative art of writing characters with brush and ink. Narita-san is home to the Naritasan Calligraphy Museum, one of Japan’s leading museums devoted to the art, and the temple offers shakyo (sutra copying), where visitors trace or brush a Buddhist sutra in quiet concentration as a form of prayer and mindfulness. Hands-on brush workshops let you grind ink, learn the basic strokes and create your own piece to take home.

item.title: Naritasan Setsubun Guide: Bean-Throwing Festival & Access
item.description: Each February 3rd, Narita-san Shinshoji Temple hosts one of Japan’s most famous Setsubun celebrations — the bean-throwing ritual that drives out bad luck and welcomes spring. From a special stage, costumed participants hurl roasted soybeans (and lucky packets) to huge crowds shouting the traditional cry, and Narita-san is renowned for its celebrity guests: famous sumo grand champions, NHK taiga drama actors and other stars take part, drawing big crowds and national TV coverage.

item.title: Nomizo Falls & Kameiwa Cave Guide: Heart of Light & Access
item.description: Hidden in the forested Kiyosumi Gorge of central Boso, Nomizo Falls and the adjacent Kameiwa Cave are home to one of Chiba’s most magical natural sights. On clear mornings in the right season, sunlight streams through the cave’s tunnel-like opening and reflects off the still water below, forming a luminous, near-perfect heart shape that went viral and now draws photographers from across Japan. Even outside those golden moments, the mossy rock arch, gentle waterfall and emerald stream make a serene, fairy-tale woodland scene.

item.title: Onjuku & Southern Boso Coast Guide: Beaches & Access
item.description: The breezy resort town of Onjuku, on Chiba’s outer Boso coast, is a classic Japanese seaside escape — a crescent of white sand and turquoise shallows that has drawn beachgoers since the early 20th century. Gentle, clean and family-friendly, Onjuku Beach is great for swimming and lazing, watched over by a quirky “Tsukimi” mermaid statue and a monument commemorating the 1609 rescue of shipwrecked Spanish sailors bound for Mexico (the town’s enduring link to Acapulco).

item.title: Sawara Guide: Little Edo Canal Town, Grand Festival & Access
item.description: The merchant town of Sawara, in Katori, is the jewel of Chiba’s old townscapes — a beautifully preserved “Little Edo” where black-tiled merchant houses, willow trees and stone bridges line the Ono River canal. Once a prosperous river-trade hub, it retains a rare Edo-period atmosphere, best enjoyed on a leisurely boat ride down the canal or a stroll past its old sake breweries and the former home of Ino Tadataka, the surveyor who first mapped Japan accurately.

item.title: Tokyo Disney Resort Guide: Tickets, Parks & Access
item.description: Despite the name, Tokyo Disney Resort sits in Urayasu, Chiba, on the shore of Tokyo Bay — and it’s one of the world’s most popular theme-park destinations. The resort pairs two distinct parks: Tokyo Disneyland, the classic castle park beloved for its parades and fairy-tale lands, and Tokyo DisneySea, a uniquely Japanese, nautically themed park (found nowhere else) celebrated for its immersive harbours, detailed theming and more grown-up attractions. With resort hotels, the Ikspiari mall and the Disney Resort monorail tying it together, plus famously polished service and seasonal events, it’s an easy, dazzling day (or several) right next to Tokyo.

item.title: Yoro Valley Guide: Onsen, Autumn Leaves & Access
item.description: Tucked into the green heart of the Boso Peninsula, Yoro Valley (Yorokeikoku) is Chiba’s premier nature escape — a winding river gorge of clear pools, waterfalls and forested ridges that erupts into brilliant colour each autumn. It’s one of the latest-colouring autumn-leaf spots near Tokyo (late November to early December), and its riverside onsen ryokan let you soak among the foliage. Walking trails lead to the photogenic Awamata Falls and a curious old road tunnel, while the rural Kominato and Isumi railways make getting there half the fun.

item.title: ZOZO Marine Stadium Guide: Baseball, Bayfront & Access
item.description: Right on Tokyo Bay in the Makuhari Bayfront, ZOZO Marine Stadium is the seaside home of the Chiba Lotte Marines — and one of the most fun, accessible places for visitors to experience a Japanese pro baseball game. Japanese baseball is a spectacle as much as a sport: nonstop organised chanting, team songs, balloon launches and passionate fan sections create an electric, family-friendly atmosphere quite unlike the game in the West.

item.title: Chiba Events 2026: Fireworks, Tokyo Game Show, Gion Festivals & Disney
item.description: Chiba is where most visitors land (Narita Airport) and where Tokyo Disney Resort actually sits — but the prefecture’s own 2026 event calendar is far richer than a transit stop suggests. It hosts some of the Kanto region’s biggest summer fireworks, two UNESCO-linked Gion float festivals on the same weekend, the world’s largest video-game show, a temple-steps display of thirty thousand hina dolls, and whale-and-dolphin watching off its Pacific coast. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Chiba Family Trip: Disney, Beaches, Wildlife & Kids' Attractions
item.description: Chiba is one of the best prefectures in Japan for a family trip. It holds the country’s most visited theme park complex, a world-class aquarium, Japan’s longest beach, and a whole peninsula of coastal scenery and wildlife encounters within easy reach of Tokyo. Children aged 3 to 15 will find something genuinely exciting at almost every stop, and the prefecture’s flat terrain and excellent rail connections make logistics manageable. Tokyo Disney Resort — The Family Centrepiece For most families visiting Chiba, Tokyo Disney Resort is the main reason they came.

item.title: Chiba Food Guide: Unagi, Sashimi, Peanuts & Pacific Seafood
item.description: Chiba Prefecture sits on the Pacific and Tokyo Bay, and its food culture reflects that position directly. The prefecture produces over 80 percent of Japan’s peanuts, operates Japan’s largest fishing port at Choshi, and hosts one of the oldest unagi-dining traditions in the country along the approach road to Naritasan Temple. For overseas visitors willing to venture beyond Narita Airport’s restaurants and the Disney Resort food courts, Chiba offers some of the most distinctive and affordable culinary experiences in the entire Kanto region.

item.title: Chiba Girls' Trip: DisneySea Magic, Boso Spa Days & Fresh Market Mornings
item.description: Chiba delivers a range of girls' trip itineraries that few Japanese prefectures can match in variety. One day is Tokyo DisneySea at its most beautiful — harbour views, character encounters, cocktails at Lounge de Viento. The next is a tatami room at a Yoro Valley ryokan, steaming outdoor bath above the river, and a multi-course dinner arriving dish by dish. A third is Katsuura fish market at dawn, cut flowers from the farmstead stalls of the Boso interior, and the long Pacific beach almost entirely to yourselves.

item.title: Chiba Haunted Spots: Coastal Legends, Maritime Ghosts & Eerie Boso Landscapes
item.description: The Boso Peninsula has centuries of history as a site of maritime danger, ancient religious practice, and isolated community life. The Pacific coast produced shipwrecks that left behind stories absorbed into local tradition. The mountain trails of the interior cross ancient battle sites from the Genpei and Sengoku periods. The Yoro Valley gorge has forest dense enough to hold genuine darkness at noon. And Cape Inubosaki, where two major ocean currents meet in collision, has kept lighthouse keepers in an enforced solitude that generated its own distinctive folklore.

item.title: Chiba Hidden Gems: Beyond Narita Airport and Tokyo Disney
item.description: Most visitors to Chiba pass through Narita Airport, board a train to Tokyo, and never return. Some stop at Tokyo Disney Resort and go no further. But Chiba extends far beyond its airport and theme park — south along the Boso Peninsula, east to the lighthouse at the Pacific edge, and into an interior of forested gorges, rural railways, and fishing villages that have changed very little since the Meiji era.

item.title: Chiba Honeymoon: Boso Ryokan, DisneySea & Pacific Sunsets
item.description: Chiba is not the prefecture that first comes to mind for a honeymoon in Japan — Kyoto, Hakone, and Okinawa claim those expectations. But Chiba offers something those destinations cannot combine: the world’s most beautiful theme park on one day, and a quietly magnificent stretch of Pacific coastline with traditional ryokan on the next, all within two hours of Tokyo. The southern Boso Peninsula is genuinely romantic country — warm winters, sea views, fresh seafood, and a near-total absence of international tourist crowds.

item.title: Chiba Leisure: Tokyo Disney Resort, Surfing, Baseball & Cycling
item.description: Chiba offers an unusual spread of leisure options — from the world’s most beautiful theme park in Urayasu to the longest beach in Japan a ninety-minute drive away, and a cycling route that circles an entire peninsula. Whether you arrive chasing rides and fireworks or empty surf and coastal roads, the prefecture delivers leisure experiences that are difficult to replicate anywhere else near Tokyo. Tokyo Disney Resort — Disneyland and DisneySea Tokyo Disney Resort in Urayasu comprises two parks on Tokyo Bay: Tokyo Disneyland, which opened in 1983 as Japan’s first Western theme park, and Tokyo DisneySea, which opened in 2001 and is consistently rated among the most beautifully designed theme parks in the world.

item.title: Chiba Nature Guide: Kujukuri Beach, Boso Peninsula & Coastal Landscapes
item.description: Chiba Prefecture is the closest coastal wilderness to Tokyo — a long peninsula curling into the Pacific with 66 kilometres of unbroken sandy beach on one side, dramatic cliffs and fishing villages on the other, and a forested interior largely unknown to foreign visitors. Its natural landscapes shift with the seasons in ways that reward return visits: winter flower fields, spring rapeseed and cherry blossoms along a country railway line, summer surf beaches, and autumn foliage in the gorge country of the central hills.

item.title: Chiba Onsen Guide: Yoro Valley, Boso Peninsula & Hidden Hot Springs
item.description: Chiba is not Japan’s most famous onsen prefecture — that designation belongs to places like Gunma, Oita, or Aomori. But what Chiba lacks in volcanic drama it compensates with location: its hot springs are often the closest genuine onsen experience to central Tokyo, and its best ryokan offer something that the more tourist-heavy resort towns cannot — genuine quietness. The Yoro Valley gorge, the southern Boso Peninsula coast, and the fishing villages of the Pacific shore each have their own onsen character, and all are accessible on a weekend from the capital.

item.title: Chiba Power Spots: Sacred Shrines, Ancient Temples & Spiritual Landscapes
item.description: Chiba Prefecture sits at a significant intersection in Japan’s spiritual geography. The Boso Peninsula was one of the last parts of the Kanto region to come under central authority, and its forested interior sheltered religious traditions that predate the Nara period. At the northern end, Naritasan commands one of the largest religious followings in the country. At the tip of the Boso, ancient clan shrines maintain rituals practiced without interruption for over a thousand years.

item.title: Chiba Solo Travel Guide: From Narita Layovers to Boso Peninsula Exploration
item.description: Chiba suits solo travel well. Its public transport is good for the main routes, its food culture is built around single-person dining (fish market counters, unagi lunch sets, fishing port izakaya), and its most interesting experiences — temple walking, coastal cycling, a dawn fish market — are better done alone than in groups. For travellers arriving through Narita, it is also the most immediately accessible prefecture in Japan. Making the Most of a Narita Layover Narita Airport is in Chiba Prefecture, and the area around it offers one of the most accessible cultural experiences in Japan for travellers with time between flights.

item.title: Top Sightseeing in Chiba: Naritasan, Nokogiri-yama & the Boso Peninsula
item.description: Chiba wraps around the east side of Tokyo Bay and extends far into the Pacific, forming a prefecture that most international visitors enter — through Narita Airport — and immediately leave. That is a mistake. Within Chiba’s borders you will find one of Japan’s most-visited Buddhist temples, a cliff-face Buddha larger than the one at Nara, a coastal town that turns its stone staircases into a river of traditional dolls each spring, and a forested gorge whose cave produces one of Japan’s most photographed natural phenomena.

item.title: Best Hotels & Ryokan in Chiba: Tokyo Disney, Narita & Boso Peninsula
item.description: Chiba Prefecture surrounds much of greater Tokyo and serves three very different traveller needs: Tokyo Disney Resort (the most-visited theme park in Asia), Narita Airport hotels (for transit and early-departure stays), and the Boso Peninsula (a dramatic Pacific coastline with fishing villages, flower fields, and surf beaches largely unknown to foreign visitors). Best Areas to Stay Maihama (Tokyo Disney Resort) The Disney area — Maihama Station is the gateway to Tokyo Disneyland and DisneySea.
